> **What this case shows** — a mechanistic generator is only credible if it
> reproduces *reality*, not just if it oscillates plausibly on its own. Here the
> **Jansen-Rit** neural-mass model — a single cortical column of coupled neural
> populations — is validated against a **real** eyes-closed occipital EEG
> (PhysioNet eegmmidb, subject S001). The real channel has a **10.0 Hz alpha peak**
> carrying 67% of its 1–40 Hz power; the generic Jansen-Rit column emits alpha at
> **10.75 Hz**, and scaling its membrane time constants ×0.96 to the real alpha
> frequency puts the model's peak at **10.0 Hz**, with alpha the dominant band in
> both. A bare column *over-concentrates* power in alpha (relative alpha 0.99 vs the
> real 0.67); adding a physiological **1/f (aperiodic) background** spreads power off
> the peak and brings the model's relative alpha to **0.65**, matching the real 0.67
> — so both the peak *and* the broadband spectral shape line up. This is the
> **validation-against-reality** tier, distinct from the synthetic-data recovery that
> only *verifies* an estimator. **How to read it** — left, the real and
> personalised-model power spectra overlaid, both peaking in the alpha band; right, a
> strip of the personalised generator's alpha rhythm.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — to validate a mechanistic rhythm generator against real data:
measure the real signal's **spectral peak** and **band structure**, **personalise**
the model's physical parameters (here the membrane time constants to the measured
peak, and the **1/f background amplitude** to the measured relative band power), then
check the model reproduces the peak frequency, the band dominance and the broadband
spectral shape.
**Way of thinking** — "the generator recovers its own parameters on synthetic data"
is **verification of the estimator**; "the generator, tuned to a subject, reproduces
that subject's real rhythm" is **validation of the model** — a different, stronger
claim, and the one that makes an in-silico experiment trustworthy. It is a claim
about the emergent **rhythm**, not the exact stochastic waveform.
**Ecosystem usage** — `jansenRit()` (PhysioTwin) as the neural-mass generator, with
its `aperiodic=` argument (`aperiodicNoise()`) adding the physiological 1/f floor;
`bandPower()` for the band structure; the same personalise-then-compare protocol
validates any mechanistic rhythm generator against real recordings.
:::

## Proposition

The mechanistic Jansen-Rit model reproduces a real EEG's alpha rhythm: a real
eyes-closed occipital channel peaks at 10.0 Hz (relative alpha power 0.67), the
generic model peaks at 10.75 Hz, and personalising the membrane time constants
(×0.96) matches the real peak at 10.0 Hz — with alpha the dominant band in both.

## Question & goal

**The question is model credibility, not code correctness.** A digital twin's
in-silico predictions are only worth trusting if the underlying generator matches
reality. A model oscillating at "about 10 Hz" on synthetic settings verifies the
*implementation*; it says nothing about whether the *model* matches a brain. We ask
the harder question: does the mechanistic column, tuned to a real subject's alpha
frequency, reproduce that subject's actual resting EEG rhythm?

## Challenge & approach

We take an eyes-closed occipital channel (O1) of eegmmidb subject S001, run R02,
and compute its power spectrum (Welch, 8 s segments): the dominant frequency in
1–40 Hz and the relative alpha (8–13 Hz) power. We then generate `jansenRit()`,
compute the same summaries the same way, and **personalise** the model in two steps:
first scale its excitatory/inhibitory membrane time constants until the model's alpha
peak matches the real one, then fit the amplitude of a physiological **1/f (aperiodic)
background** (`jansenRit(aperiodic=)`) until the model's relative alpha matches the
real one — a bare cortical column carries only its own rhythm, whereas a real scalp
channel sits on a broadband 1/f floor.

## Data

**eegmmidb S001R02**, channel O1 (Schalk et al., PhysioNet) — 61 s eyes-closed
resting EEG @ 160 Hz. Details in [`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![The real EEG power spectrum (blue) and the personalised Jansen-Rit spectrum
(red), both peaking in the 8–13 Hz alpha band (grey dashed); right, a strip of the
personalised generator's alpha rhythm.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* the mechanistic column already produces alpha near the right
frequency (10.75 Hz); scaling the membrane time constants — the neural mass's
personalisation — pulls its peak onto the real 10.0 Hz, and adding the fitted 1/f
background spreads its power off the peak so the relative alpha matches the real
value too. Alpha is the dominant band in both spectra.

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| real alpha peak | 10.0 Hz |
| Jansen-Rit alpha, generic | 10.75 Hz |
| Jansen-Rit alpha, **personalised** | **10.0 Hz** |
| relative alpha — real | 0.67 |
| relative alpha — model, bare column | 0.99 (over-concentrated) |
| relative alpha — model, **+ fitted 1/f background** (×1.8 SD) | **0.65** (matches real) |
| alpha the dominant band (real / model) | yes / yes |

## Conclusion

The mechanistic Jansen-Rit model, tuned to a real subject's alpha frequency and
sat on a fitted physiological 1/f background, reproduces both that subject's emergent
alpha rhythm *and* its broadband spectral shape — the model is **validated against
reality**, not merely verified on synthetic settings. The transferable takeaway:
**separate verifying the estimator (synthetic recovery) from validating the model
(tune to a subject, reproduce their real rhythm) — and be explicit that the claim
is about the emergent rhythm and spectral shape, not the exact waveform, and that the
1/f amplitude here is calibrated to the record rather than emergent from the mechanism.**

## Open questions

- The **1/f background** that now reproduces the broadband spectrum is *fit* to the
  record (its amplitude tuned to the real relative alpha); coupling several columns
  (Jansen-Rit networks) would let that aperiodic floor **emerge from the mechanism**
  instead of being calibrated. Validating across many **subjects, channels and
  eyes-open/closed states** would then map the model's domain of applicability.
  *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| step | function | package |
|---|---|---|
| generate a mechanistic EEG | `jansenRit()` | PhysioTwin |
| add a physiological 1/f background | `jansenRit(aperiodic=)` / `aperiodicNoise()` | PhysioTwin |
| relative band power | `bandPower()` | PhysioTwin |
| validity harness (V&V report) | `validateTwin()` | PhysioTwin |
